newsitem.title: USA: Clinton readies for negative debate.
newsitem.headline: Clinton readies for negative debate.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Tuesday readied for personal attacks in his final debate with Republican Bob Dole, as his aides predicted Dole will lose votes to third-party rival Ross Perot if he turns mean spirited.

With Dole escalating his attacks on the ethics of Clinton and those around him, Clinton has been bracing for negative attacks when he and the Republican challenger meet for their final televised debate Wednesday in San Diego.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said that in practice sessions, former Sen. George Mitchell has been filling the role of Dole and "found it very hard not to cross over that line" that made negative attacks too personal."
The Maine Democrat, who has been Clinton's special envoy to resolve the tensions in Northern Ireland, has known Dole a long time and is familiar with his style and mannerisms.
Dole has been using more negative rhetoric in recent days and has vowed to bring it with him to their last debate before the Nov. 5 election.

The first two debates, the first between Clinton and Dole and the second involving vice presidential contenders Al Gore and Jack Kemp, for the most part avoided personal attacks. They also failed to have any significant impact on the lead Clinton has enjoyed for months.
"This may turn nasty," a senior campaign official said. "We're certainly getting ready for it."
White House Political Director Doug Sosnik insisted that a negative approach by Dole would only cost him votes on Election Day, with Reform Party candidate Perot the beneficiary.

He said that "having Dole pretty much completely abandon even the pretext of a positive message of why you should vote for him" would turn off voters and "the beneficiary of that would probably be Perot."

"I think he'll probably do something that Perot has not been able to do, which is to push his numbers up" in opinion polls, Sosnick said. Perot, whose independent candidacy four years ago generated considerable support, has been unable to create much interest this time around.

Clinton's ties to Indonesian James Riady have been fiercely attacked by Republicans in recent days, who suspect Riady's influence is behind big contributions to the Democratic Party from individuals with links to an Indonesian financial conglomerate, the Lippo Group.

Dole's campaign theme Tuesday was on character issues involving Clinton and his those around him -- challenging the president's assertion upon coming to office that he wanted one of the most ethical administrations in history.
Just how aggressive Dole should be in the final debate -- likely to be watched by some 70 million Americans -- has been a subject of disagreement among his strategists.
In 1976, when Dole was the Republican vice presidential nominee, his confrontational style contributed to incumbent President Gerald Ford's defeat at the hands of Democrat Jimmy Carter.
Dole has spent much of the campaign season trying to soften the lingering image of him as a "hatchet man," and at least some of his advisers have argued against him leading the attack on Clinton.
Clinton arrived in New Mexico Sunday and has been practicing twice a day for his 90-minute exchange with Dole. They will take questions from an audience of undecided voters.
Clinton interrupted his schedule to meet with the author of a study that found that the amount of violence on network television has been declining.
